author: gabrielburagev
body:
## Problem

`package.json` pins two native rolldown bindings exactly:

```json
"@rolldown/binding-darwin-arm64": "1.2.0",
"@rolldown/binding-linux-x64-gnu": "1.2.0",
```

They were added in `ci: fix publishing [WEB-2982]` (#892) so both platforms' binaries resolve, and `tsdown` is what actually owns the rolldown version.

Dependabot currently bumps each binding on its own schedule, independently of `tsdown`. That's a problem because `rolldown` pins its `@rolldown/binding-*` optionalDependencies to an **exact** version — `rolldown@1.2.0` requires `@rolldown/binding-*@1.2.0`. So a binding bumped by itself gets installed *alongside* the version rolldown actually loads, not instead of it:

```diff
-  '@rolldown/binding-darwin-arm64@1.2.0': {}
+  '@rolldown/binding-darwin-arm64@1.2.0':
+    optional: true
+
+  '@rolldown/binding-darwin-arm64@1.2.6': {}
```

rolldown resolves its binding from its own subtree and keeps loading `1.2.0`. The newer pin becomes a second native binary nothing loads, and the pin no longer reflects the bundler in use — defeating the point of pinning it.

This isn't hypothetical churn: there have been ~20 separate binding PRs since January (#918, #940, #943, #958, #961, #990, #1019, #1023, #1026, #1059, #1061, #1130, #1131, #1144, #1145, #1152, #1155, #1164, #1168, #1185), alternating between the two platforms and never in step with `tsdown`.

Worth noting the skew is invisible to CI — the build check is `tsc --noEmit`, so the real tsdown/rolldown bundle never runs on a PR.

## Change

Adds a `bundler` group to `.github/dependabot.yaml` alongside the existing `types` group:

```yaml
      bundler:
        patterns:
          - 'tsdown'
          - 'rolldown'
          - '@rolldown/*'
```

`tsdown` and both bindings now arrive in a single PR, so they move together and any version skew is visible in one diff instead of spread across separate PRs landing weeks apart.

## Notes

- Grouping rather than ignoring: the pins are load-bearing for the publish workflow, so they should keep updating — just in lockstep.
- This makes skew *reviewable*, not impossible. If a grouped PR still shows a binding ahead of what `rolldown` requires, that's the signal to hold it until `tsdown` catches up.
- Currently open #1204 and #1207 (both now `1.2.0 → 1.2.6`) are exactly this case and can be closed in favour of the first grouped PR.

Config verified to parse, with the existing `types` group and all other settings preserved; `prettier --check` passes.

This adds automated, approved USD Plaid depository feeds to the existing cash reconciliation workflow. author: wsunicorn
body:
Bảng trung tâm của chương 7. Viết thành script chứ không gõ tay, vì lý do dưới đây.

## Vì sao phải là script

Cột chi phí đến từ **hai file đo hai thứ khác nhau, và cả hai đều đặt tên `ms_per_sample`**:

| File | Nghĩa là gì | Độ lớn |
|---|---|---|
| `results/runs.jsonl` | thời gian **bộ phân loại** — hồi quy logistic, chạy CPU | 0,001–0,013 ms |
| `results/feasibility.jsonl` | thời gian **lượt đọc** để lấy ma trận chú ý | 222–608 ms |

Chênh **năm bậc độ lớn**. Một dòng lấy nhầm cột trông vẫn hợp lý và lật ngược kết luận chương 7 —
nó sẽ nói hướng nội tại nhanh hơn XLM-R hai nghìn lần.

## Bảng 8 — kết quả

| Phương pháp | macro-F1 | ms/mẫu | VRAM | Tham số |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline bề mặt (E01) | 0,6562 | **0,001** | — | **9** |
| Gemini giám khảo (E10) | 0,6637 | 8.194,0 | — | 0 |
| PhoBERT-large (E09) | 0,7487 | 12,3 | 9.002 MB | 369.166.339 |
| XLM-R-large (E09) | **0,7762** | 25,2 | 11.231 MB | 559.893.507 |
| Lookback gộp 7B (E02) | 0,7451 | 437,6 | 8.328 MB | 2.271 |
| Chunk-aware 7B (E03) | 0,7567 | 437,6 | 8.328 MB | 579 |
| **Lookback gộp 3B (E14)** | 0,7345 | **222,7** | **3.710 MB** | **195** |
| Chunk-aware 3B (E14) | 0,7217 | 222,7 | 3.710 MB | 1.851 |
| Lookback gộp 1.5B (E14) | 0,7232 | 608,1 | 2.718 MB | 1.011 |
| Chunk-aware 1.5B (E14) | 0,7345 | 608,1 | 2.718 MB | 1.131 |
| Sailor2-8B (E13), hai dòng | 0,7377 / 0,7120 | *chưa đo* | *chưa đo* | 195 / 1.155 |

**XLM-R thắng cả hai trục tuyệt đối** — cao hơn 0,0195 điểm và nhanh hơn **17 lần** dòng
chunk-aware tốt nhất. Không có cách đọc nào biến bảng này thành "hướng nội tại rẻ hơn về thời
gian tuyệt đối". Viết đúng như vậy.

**Chỗ hướng nội tại thắng là số tham số:** lookback gộp trên Qwen2.5-3B đạt 0,7345 với **đúng 195
tham số**, so với **559.893.507** của XLM-R — ít hơn **2,87 triệu lần**, mất 0,0417 điểm. Và 195
tham số thì huấn luyện trên CPU trong vài giây, không có rủi ro không hội tụ như InfoXLM ở E09.

**Nấc 3B là điểm cân bằng của cả bảng.**

## Cột chi phí biên: đã lượng hóa, vẫn là giả thiết

Chi phí biên 0,002–0,010 ms tách thành cột riêng có nhãn. **Không thí nghiệm nào trong đề tài đo
được nó** — nó đòi hệ RAG đầu cuối, mà T40 mới dựng.

Và có một khoản biên **thật mà chưa ai đo**: bật `output_attentions` vô hiệu hóa FlashAttention,
nên hệ RAG đang dùng FlashAttention phải trả thêm để lấy được ma trận chú ý.

## Hai ô của Bảng 1 sai

Bảng 1 ghi E02 tốn **464 ms** và E03 tốn **528 ms**. Hai dòng đọc **chung shard `8c49fc0417f1`**,
chung `extraction_hash`, tức **chung một lượt chạy mô hình đọc**. Một lượt trích không có hai giá.

Chênh 64 ms là nhiễu giữa hai phép đo, bị đọc nhầm thành "chunk-aware đắt hơn lookback" — và nó
đã nằm trong **báo cáo giữa kỳ**. Lượt xen kẽ T31 cho **437,6 ms** cho cả hai, trôi 2,09 %.

Quy tắc rút ra, nay có test khóa: **hai dòng chung `extraction_hash` phải chung ô chi phí.**

## Tiêu chí hoàn thành

```
$ python scripts/build_tradeoff.py
  số dòng            : 12/12
  Đã ghi results/tradeoff.csv — 12 dòng

  Chưa đo chi phí, để trống thay vì mượn số của mô hình khác:
    - Lookback gộp, Sailor2-8B (E13)
    - Chunk-aware, Sailor2-8B (E13)

$ python -m ruff check .
All checks passed!
$ python -m pytest -q
721 passed
```

body:
Ada dua hal yang dijual, dan cuma satu di antaranya kena margin.

| | Harga | Margin |
|---|---|---|
| **Akses platform** — sekali bayar, 20 tahun | Rp 7.500.000 (1 user) · Rp 15.000.000 (3 user) | tidak ada, rupiah apa adanya |
| **Saldo AI** — dibeli terpisah | kurs jual `forex / (1 − margin/100)` = Rp 25.714/USD | **30%** |

Karena itu `credit_grant_usd` kedua paket = **0**. Paket ini menjual akses, bukan kredit. Menaruh jatah kredit di paket akan menghitung margin dua kali: sekali diam-diam di harga paket, sekali lagi saat pelanggan membeli saldo.

Rangkaiannya tetap utuh tanpa kode tambahan: paket berjatah 0 membiarkan `billing_mode` di `byo_key`, lalu **top-up saldo pertama** yang memindahkan pelanggan ke mode kredit — `grant_credit` sudah menyalakannya saat `credit_since` masih kosong. Jadi "generate memotong saldo" bekerja dengan sendirinya; yang perlu dilakukan cuma tidak menaruh angka di tempat yang salah.

## Yang berubah

| Kode | Label | Durasi | Harga | Kredit | Kursi | Aktif |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lifetime` | Lifetime — 1 user | 240 bln (20 th) | Rp 7.500.000 | 0 | 1 | ✓ |
| `team3` | Lifetime — 3 user | 240 bln (20 th) | Rp 15.000.000 | 0 | 3 | ✓ |
| `annual` | Tahunan | 12 bln | — | 0 | 1 | ✗ |

**Lifetime dibetulkan dari 300 bulan jadi 240.** Definisinya 20 tahun. Selisih lima tahun pada paket yang dijual sekali seumur hidup bukan pembulatan — ia lima tahun akses yang tidak pernah dibayar, dan tidak ada yang akan menyadarinya sampai tahun ke-21.

**Paket tahunan dinonaktifkan.** Ia tidak punya harga. Webhook memang tidak bisa mencocokkannya (`price_idr` NULL tidak pernah cocok), tapi ia tetap muncul di pilihan "tambah manual" — dan sekali terpilih, ia memberi 12 bulan akses tanpa ada pembayaran yang pernah tercatat. Dinonaktifkan, bukan dihapus: kalau suatu hari dijual lagi, harganya tinggal diisi.

**`lifetime` dipakai ulang, bukan diganti kode baru.** Sudah ada langganan yang menunjuk ke kode itu (workspace operator dari backfill `0037`), dan mengganti kodenya akan memutus baris tersebut.

## Utang yang belum lunas

`max_seats` disimpan di paket (1 dan 3) tapi **belum ditegakkan di mana pun**. Hari ini setiap pendaftar mendapat workspace sendiri lewat trigger `handle_new_user`, dan tidak ada jalur untuk bergabung ke workspace orang lain — jadi "3 user" belum bisa terjadi bahkan kalau paketnya dibeli.

Ini harus lunas **sebelum** pelanggan paket 3 user yang pertama dilayani, bukan sesudahnya: sesudahnya berarti ada orang yang sudah membayar Rp 15.000.000 untuk sesuatu yang belum ada. Angkanya disimpan lebih dulu supaya kebijakannya punya satu tempat tinggal saat jalur undangannya dibangun.

author: rainmanjam
body:
The committed shots were taken **27 August**, before #766 landed one palette and one type scale across both surfaces. Every screenshot in the README, the docs and the website's feature pages was showing the product as it looked before the thing that most changed how it looks.

**21 of 22 regenerated** from a live install with a real synthetic stream, plus the tour video. `web/src/assets/shots` is the website's copy of ten of them and `capture-media.sh` keeps it in step, so those move together and `features-shots.test.ts` still passes.

`08-mix-matrix.png` is unchanged, and honestly so: its test skips when no destination on the capture install uses the mix matrix, which is the case today. The file is stale and the guard says why, rather than quietly shipping a shot of something else.

## The capture's credential guard was failing safe, and wrong

`sources` aborted on *"the tokens were never found on the page to mask"*.

The mask sweeps text nodes and input values, and it found nothing to sweep — because `SecretCode` now renders `"•".repeat(16)` and puts the real value in the DOM only when the operator reveals it. **The page had become safer, and the assertion protecting it started failing**, blocking `05-sources.png` from ever being refreshed again.

That assertion was reading a proxy — *"did I mask something?"* — rather than the property, which is *"is a live credential visible in this shot?"*. `assertNoTokenSurvived` already checks the property directly, after the shutter, against both the page text and every field value. A field that moves and leaks fails **that**, whether or not the sweep hit anything.

So `hits > 0` is not deleted, it is demoted:

| | |
|---|---|
| `tokens > 0` | **kept** — fails if the API stops handing out credentials to look for, which would make everything below vacuous |
| the mask sweep | **kept** — a future page may well print a token in plain text again |
| `hits > 0` | **demoted to a log line** — no longer has to succeed for the shot to be taken |
| `assertNoTokenSurvived` | **unchanged, and now the sole control** — checked after the shutter |

Same shape as the guard findings earlier this week: the check read a proxy for the thing it cared about, and went red when the proxy stopped being true while the property still held.

author: nwparker
body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 3 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​323 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​1 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​322 |
| Prod | 4 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​229 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​13 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​216 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Every time you update Orca, the relay that runs on your SSH host gets installed into a **new folder whose name is a hash of the app's bytes**. The relay listens on a socket *inside* that folder. So after an update, the new Orca looks in a new folder, finds no socket, and starts a **second** relay — while the old one keeps running forever, still holding every terminal and every agent you had open. They are not dead. They are unreachable. One field host had 11 folders, 11 sockets, and 19 orphans.

The reason it works this way is that `RELAY_VERSION` is the frozen string `'0.1.0'` and has never moved, so the content hash was added to tell builds apart. But a hash answers "are these the same bytes?", and the question that actually matters is "**can these two talk to each other?**" — which is almost always yes, because a rebuild changes bytes without changing the wire.

This PR gives the relay a real answer to the second question: an integer `RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, offered as a range in the handshake. A relay now accepts a bridge from a *different build* as long as that bridge says it can speak a protocol the relay speaks. The byte-hash comparison stays as the fallback for every peer that offers no range.

This is the same mechanism the local terminal daemon has always used (`src/main/daemon/daemon-protocol-version.ts`), where 35 earlier protocol versions stay attachable across an update.

## One value doing three jobs

The build hash is a legitimate **artifact** identity — "are these the same bytes?" — that has been pressed into service as two other identities it was never fit for:

| identity | question it answers | what should carry it |
|---|---|---|
| **artifact** | are these the same bytes? | the content hash — correct today |
| **endpoint** | which socket do I dial? | the install path — still the hash (Release N+1) |
| **protocol** | can these two drive each other? | `RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION` — **this PR** |

Splitting the three is the fix. Release N introduces the protocol one and leaves the other two exactly as they are.

## This is Release N of two

The relay already deployed on a user's host **never updates itself**. So tolerance has to ship one release *before* any client can use it.

- **This release (N):** the relay learns to *accept* a cross-build peer. No client behaviour changes at all — nothing in this build ever points a bridge at another version's socket, so the new code path is dormant until N+1.
- **Release N+1:** the client learns to *find* a stranded relay and route to it, and the hash-equality gates can start to retire.

**The update *to* this release still strands once, unavoidably.** The relay that gets orphaned by installing this build is the *old* one, which does not have this code. Nothing shipped now can reach back and fix that. From N+1 onward, it stops.

## What changed

- `src/shared/relay-protocol-version.ts` (new) — `RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, `MIN_RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, and `relayProtocolOfferAdmits()`.
- `src/relay/protocol.ts` — three existing handshake arms gain optional fields: `protocolVersion` / `minProtocolVersion` on all three, and `capabilities` on `orca-relay-handshake-ok`.
- `src/relay/relay-handshake.ts` — the daemon admits a peer when *either* the build hash matches (unchanged) *or* the peer's offered range contains this relay's protocol version (new). Replies now carry the relay's own range and capabilities.

### Why a range and not a version number

Reviewers reach for a single integer first, and it does not work here. **The stranded relay is by construction the *older* side**, and the handshake's first frame is the first thing on the wire — there is no earlier round trip in which a newer client could learn what to downgrade to. So the *client* states a range and the *relay* checks whether it falls inside it. That lets an old relay say yes immediately, which is the whole point: the relay that needs to accept is the one that can never be updated.

### Deliberately not changed

- **Exit 42, `RelayVersionMismatchError`, the PTY grant `serverBuildId` check, and owner-claim recovery all stay.** They are Release N+1's to retire.
- **The socket stays inside the version directory.** GC reads liveness from in there (`remote-install-gc.ts`), so moving it would break reclamation.
- **No client-side relay router.** Out of scope for this release.

## Wire compatibility

`docs/reference/remote-wire-compatibility.md` Rule 1 — new optional fields on frames that already ship. `parseHandshakeMessage` throws on an unknown `type` and the throw closes the socket, so a new message *type* was never an option; `endpointCredential?` is the existing precedent for growing an arm.

**What an old relay does with the new optional fields:** ignores them. Its `parseHandshakeMessage` validates only `type` and returns the object; unknown keys are never read. It then compares build hashes exactly as before and refuses on mismatch, exit 42. Verified on a real host — see scenario A below.

**What a new relay sends to an old client:** an `orca-relay-handshake-ok` carrying two extra numbers and a `capabilities` object. The old bridge parses it, reads only `type` and `version`, and connects normally. Verified on a real host below: exit 0, and its log line simply lacks the `protocol=` field it cannot read.

**No new opcode** (Rule 2 does not apply — `MessageType` is untouched). **Nothing the relay already published changed meaning** (Rule 3): the fields are purely additive and every reader treats them as optional.

## SSH execution boundary

`docs/reference/ssh-execution-boundary.md` already documents this bug by name and points at the daemon model as the fix. Nothing here kills anything or infers a verdict: this change only ever *admits* a connection that would previously have been refused. A stranded relay holding live PTYs stays `live` — the direction is leak, never kill.

## Proof — real hosts, real bundles

Two relay bundles built from two different commits (`origin/main` at 2bf298d1dc1, and this branch), installed into version directories named exactly like production, sockets bound inside them. Not simulated.

**Linux (`openclaw`, Ubuntu, node v26):**

```
A. BASELINE — pre-Release-N daemon, later-build bridge, hashes differ
   exit=42
   [relay-connect] Handshake mismatch: expected=0.1.0+aaaa…, daemon=0.1.0+cccc…, daemonProtocol=none, ours=1; exiting 42
   daemon still listening after refusal: yes          <-- this is #13852, and why updating TO N strands once

B. THE FIX — Release-N daemon, later-build bridge, hashes differ
   exit=0
   [relay] Handshake OK from version=0.1.0+cccc… (cross-build, protocol 1)

C. UNCHANGED PATH — Release-N daemon, same-build bridge
   exit=0
```

**Wire compat, both skew directions, same host:**

```
NEW RELAY -> OLD CLIENT   exit=0   [relay-connect] Handshake OK at version=0.1.0+shared
NEW RELAY -> NEW CLIENT   exit=0   [relay-connect] Handshake OK at version=0.1.0+shared protocol=1
```

**Windows (`awin`, node v24):** the handshake suites run there against real Windows **named pipes** (`relayTestSocketPath` returns `\\.\pipe\…` on win32) — 25/25 pass, including the cross-build acceptance. Windows matters here because its pipe name hashes the version folder and the superseded sweep is a no-op there, so Windows orphans are not even logged today; this change is transport-agnostic and behaves identically.

author: nagasatish007
body:
# Problem

The README and docs consistently use the top-level import form:

```python
from tealtiger import TealEngine, PolicyMode, DecisionAction, ReasonCode
```

…but `TealEngine`, `TealGuard`, `TealAudit`, and `TealCircuit` were only importable from `tealtiger.core` — they were never re-exported in the package's `__init__.py`. So the documented import raises:

```
ImportError: cannot import name 'TealEngine' from 'tealtiger'
```

This affects the **published PyPI README** (the first snippet a new user copies), the v1.4 docs, the package's own `policy_tester.py` docstring, and ~20 integration examples across the ecosystem. It's the kind of bug that only surfaces the moment someone runs the quickstart.

Two smaller issues were fixed in the same file while here:
- `observe`, `freeze`, `unfreeze`, `FrozenAgentError`, and `UnsupportedProviderError` were imported but missing from `__all__` (5 pre-existing `F401` lint errors).
- `__version__` was stale at `"1.0.0"` while the package ships as `1.4.0`.

## Change

`src/tealtiger/__init__.py` only (+29/-1):
- Re-export the core governance classes at the top level: `TealEngine`, `TealGuard`, `TealAudit`, `TealAuditConfig`, `TealCircuit`, `CircuitState`, `CircuitOpenError`, `RedactionLevel`.
- Add the `observe()` entry points (`observe`, `freeze`, `unfreeze`, `FrozenAgentError`, `UnsupportedProviderError`) to `__all__`.
- Correct `__version__` to `1.4.0`.

No behavioral change — purely surfacing already-public classes at the documented import path.

## Verification

- `from tealtiger import TealEngine, TealGuard, TealAudit, TealCircuit` now succeeds (previously `ImportError`).
- `from tealtiger import PolicyMode, DecisionAction, ReasonCode, PolicyBuilder, CostTracker` continues to work.
- `ruff check` — clean.
- `__all__` has no dangling names; 70 public exports.
- Test suite: **416 passed** across `tests/core`, `tests/test_guardrails.py`, `tests/test_guardrail_engine.py`, and `tests/observe`. (The two `tests/integrations/test_google_adk*` collection errors are pre-existing and unrelated — they require the optional `agentops` dependency.)

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

Several docs import `GovernancePolicy` / `GovernanceMode` **from `tealtiger`**, which are not part of this package at all (that's the AG2 extension's API — `ag2_tealtiger` / `ag2.extensions.tealtiger`). Those doc snippets need separate per-file correction and are tracked outside this change.

- verifies the target Supabase function inventory reports every required slug as `ACTIVE`
- attests only `core_schema_ready`, `runtime_secret_ready`, and `function_inventory_ready`
- keeps Google/WhatsApp/AI re-key readiness, scheduler, autonomous outbound, execution runtime, replication readiness, and auto-failover fail-closed
- adds CI for dependency closure/path safety and pinned entrypoint existence
- adds a dedicated production deploy workflow for `h-standby-runtime-config`, because the general runtime deploy workflow did not deploy this function

## Security / failover invariants
- Supabase and GitHub provisioning tokens remain one-time and are never persisted
- management token now explicitly needs `database:write`, `edge_functions:write`, and `edge_functions:read`
- deployment alone cannot enable failover
- re-key readiness flags remain false until identity/provider key continuity is implemented and verified

## Why
The previous execution contract correctly blocked failover but the function-inventory dimension was not implemented, and `h-standby-runtime-config` did not have a deployment workflow. This PR makes that readiness dimension real and verifiable without claiming the standby is executable yet.

body:
## 왜

`More entries, more chances to win` 이라 **한 사람이 여러 판을 제출하는 게 정상 흐름**입니다.
그때마다 같은 호출이 나가면 폼 자동화(쿠폰 배포·단발 메일 발송)가 다시 실행될 수 있습니다.

Kajabi 가 연락처는 이메일로 합쳐 주고 이메일 시퀀스도 재구독시키지 않지만, 그건 폼 자동화 설정에 달렸습니다.
앱에서 거는 편이 확실합니다.

## 판단 기준

**"이 이메일로 제출한 적 있나" 가 아니라 "이 이메일을 Kajabi 에 넘긴 적 있나" 입니다.**
(Optional) 체크를 껐다 켰다 할 수 있어서, 제출 이력으로 세면 처음 체크한 판을 놓칩니다.

| 제출 | Optional | 동작 |
|---|---|---|
| 1번째 | ☐ | 안 보냄 |
| 2번째 | ☑ | **보냄** |
| 3번째 | ☑ | 건너뜀 |
| 4번째 | ☐ | 안 보냄 |

## 무엇을

`race_scores.kajabi_synced_at` 에 넘긴 시각을 남기고 **성공했을 때만** 채웁니다.

- 중복 제출이 걸러집니다
- **실패한 사람을 SQL 한 줄로 뽑을 수 있습니다** — 토큰이 만료돼 끊겨도 고친 뒤 밀린 사람만 다시 보내면 됩니다
- 로그를 안 봐도 연동이 끊겼는지 DB 에서 보입니다

```sql
select distinct email, nickname from race_scores
where consent_marketing and kajabi_synced_at is null;
```

## 배포 순서 ⚠️

**머지 전에** Supabase SQL Editor 에서 `supabase/migration-kajabi-sync.sql` 을 먼저 실행해야 합니다.
컬럼이 없는 상태로 새 코드가 뜨면 조회가 실패합니다 (그때는 안전한 쪽 = 보내는 쪽으로 떨어지지만,
중복 방지가 동작하지 않습니다).

## 검증 중에 잡은 것

로컬 Postgres 16 으로 실제 시나리오를 돌려 보니 **위 "밀린 사람" 질의가 틀리게 나왔습니다.**

이미 Kajabi 에 들어간 사람이 또 체크하고 제출하면 그 행은 건너뛰느라 `kajabi_synced_at` 이 null 로
남아서, 멀쩡히 구독 중인 사람이 계속 "아직 못 넘긴 사람" 으로 잡혔습니다. 그대로 뒀으면 나중에
복구 SQL 을 돌릴 때 필요 없는 사람까지 다시 밀어 넣을 뻔했습니다.

**건너뛰는 경우에도 그 행에 시각을 찍도록 고쳤습니다.** 다시 확인한 결과:

- 미체크 제출 → `hasSynced` false, 대상 아님
- 체크 제출(처음) → 보냄, 표시 남김. **미체크로 넣었던 행은 null 그대로** (동의한 적 없으니 맞음)
- 체크 제출(재) → 건너뜀, 표시는 남김
- 밀린 사람 질의 → 진짜 실패한 사람 **1명만** 걸림
- 마이그레이션은 **두 번 돌려도 안전**, 신규 구축(`schema.sql`)도 통과

`npx vitest run` 222 passed (신규 4건), `npm run build` 통과, lint 17건으로 기존과 동일.

author: master-storilabs
body:
## Summary

Makes the tool ready to hand to the whole team: a one-step installer and a config mode that developers never have to hand-edit.

### `install.py` — interactive, cross-platform installer

```
python install.py             # set up / reconfigure this machine
python install.py --uninstall  # remove the login autostart
```

Checks Python + git, installs the dependency, asks four questions (folder that holds your repos / your wip name / interval / enable push — all defaulted), writes `config.local.json`, registers the login autostart, and runs one verification pass.

- **Windows** — Scheduled Tasks API via `Register-ScheduledTask` in PowerShell, *not* `schtasks.exe` (which is refused without elevation for `ONLOGON` tasks on some Windows editions — hit this during testing).
- **macOS** — `~/Library/LaunchAgents` plist + `launchctl load`
- **Linux** — `~/.config/systemd/user/` unit + `systemctl --user enable --now`, with a manual fallback if systemd is absent

`bootstrap.ps1` / `bootstrap.sh` clone-or-update the repo under `$HOME` and run `install.py`, so onboarding a dev is a 3-line paste. `SETUP.md` is the developer-facing quick start.

### `scan_directories` — repo auto-discovery

New optional top-level config key:

```json
"scan_directories": ["C:/Users/you/projects"]
```

Each run, the tool watches every git repo that is one of those folders or an immediate subdirectory of one, inheriting the top-level settings. Point it at the folder holding your projects and you never edit the config again when you clone a new repo. Explicit `repositories` entries still win for per-repo overrides. `repositories` is now optional when `scan_directories` resolves to at least one repo — existing configs with only `repositories` are unaffected.

### Tests

`test_auto_checkin.py` (stdlib `unittest`, no new dependency) — 16 tests covering schedule/push validation, `scan_directories` discovery + dedup, backward-compatible config loading, and the branch/exclude helpers.

```
python -m unittest -v
```

## Test plan

- `python -m unittest` — all pass.
- `python install.py` on Windows 11 — task registered via PowerShell, scheduler runs, `--uninstall` removes it cleanly (idempotent).
- `python auto_checkin.py --config <cfg> --once` with a `scan_directories` config — discovers repos, commits + pushes wip branches as expected.
- macOS / Linux autostart paths are written from the mechanisms already documented in the README but have **not** been run on those OSes yet — worth a check on the pilot dev's machine if they're not on Windows.

author: ashhart
body:
Warm native Qwen4 QSA prefill currently dispatches at most 256 query rows at a time, even after the score, top-k and direct-index attention kernels have all run successfully. This change batches up to 1,024 independent prefill queries per call, reducing dispatch overhead while preserving the existing token selection and native attention reductions.

The wider path requires at least 1,024 queries, the supported 24-query/2-KV-head geometry with head dimension 256, four indexer heads of dimension 128, FP16/BF16, compression ratio 4, and a 2,048-token budget. All three native stages must already be proven and enabled, and their minimum-row overrides must permit the path. Explicit query widths, first-use probes, and short decode/verification calls retain their existing behavior. A single FP32 indexer score sheet is limited to 128 MiB by reducing the width as context grows; this is not a bound on total attention or model memory. If native attention rejects a widened call, execution retries at the existing portable width before allocating per-query gathered K/V.

## Reproducible component measurements

Apple M5 Max, MLX 0.32.2, native `glm_moe_dsa` extension rebuilt against the pinned nanobind 2.15.0 ABI, BF16, 2,048 query tokens, synthetic seeded inputs and precomputed pooled keys. Each arm has three warmups and 12 measured calls; control/candidate order alternates each repetition, and outputs are synchronized. The control explicitly selects 256-query tiles; the candidate uses the automatic path, with actual 1,024-query dispatches checked before timing.

| Cached K/V tokens | 256-query median | Automatic median | Latency reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 16,384 | 16.886 ms | 16.095 ms | 4.7% |
| 65,536 | 22.170 ms | 20.882 ms | 5.8% |

These numbers measure one complete QSA attention call, including indexer scoring and selection, rather than whole-model PP or decode. Full-model throughput and peak-memory confirmation on current upstream, including M3 hardware, remain outstanding; this PR is a draft for that reason.

```sh
# From the repository root, after building the native extension:
PYTHONPATH=. MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0 python benchmarks/bench_qwen4_qsa_prefill_tiles.py --key-tokens 16384
PYTHONPATH=. MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0 python benchmarks/bench_qwen4_qsa_prefill_tiles.py --key-tokens 65536
```

## Validation

The new dispatch regression failed on unmodified main because the entry point produced 256-row calls instead of the expected 1,024-row calls. Native numerical checks compare every output byte against explicit 256-query tiling at 4,096 and 65,536 K/V tokens in both FP16 and BF16, including an uneven final query tile, and assert that the widened branch actually executes. Additional cases cover unavailable/unproven/disabled kernels, row-threshold overrides, short requests, explicit widths, score-sheet bounds, and native rejection before a large portable gather.

```sh
python -m pytest -q -o addopts= -p no:cacheprovider \
  tests/test_qwen4_qsa_*.py \
  tests/test_mlx_vlm_qwen4_exp_compat.py \
  tests/test_qwen4_eager_dispatch.py
# 228 passed with the native extension enabled
```

Ruff passes for the new benchmark and tests, and `git diff --check` passes. The three existing UP033 findings on `functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)` in `qsa_fast.py` are unchanged.

author: lemmonchess333
body:
Two colour defects. One is why the rings read as three identical grey circles with nothing logged; the other is worse and was invisible from the dark theme.

## 1. The arc was theme-blind

`TodayEnergy` passed raw `THEME.macros.*` — **one fixed set for both themes**. On a white card that puts the carbs arc at **1.92:1**. That's the *filled* portion of the ring, the half that carries the reading, effectively invisible in light mode.

`useMacroPalette()` exists for exactly this and swaps to `#A16207` / `#BE185D` / `#4F7D43` there (4.92 / 6.04 / 4.83). Dark is unchanged — `text` is `accent`.

## 2. The track is now the macro's own hue at 35%

This replaces a **neutral groove that was locked** by both the component header and a test, so it's worth being exact about why the lock doesn't survive.

Its measurement tinted `THEME.macros.carbs` — the **accent** `#EAB308` — which really is capped at 1.92:1 on white *even solid*. So "yellow cannot clear it at ANY alpha" was true **of the accent** and not of the macro. Tinting the palette's theme-aware value instead resolves it. The old reasoning was right about the value it tested and wrong about the conclusion it drew from it.

Measured against `--card`, with the caller passing the theme's own palette track:

| | track @35% | arc vs card | arc vs track |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| light | 1.85 / 1.62 / 1.59 | 6.04 / 4.92 / 4.83 | 3.26 / 3.03 / 3.03 |
| dark | 1.61 / 2.20 / 1.97 | 4.62 / 8.49 / 6.67 | 2.87 / 3.86 / 3.38 |

The groove it replaces was **1.34 light / 1.48 dark**. So every macro is *more* visible than before in both themes, the arc clears the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a meaningful graphic, and filled still reads as filled against remaining.

**35% is the balance point, not a taste call**: 25% barely beats the old groove; 45% drops arc-vs-track to ~2.6 and the ring starts reading as one flat colour.

## Tests

The two locked tests are **replaced, not deleted**:

- one pins the tint and its arithmetic (`0x59` = 89/255 = 0.349),
- one pins that the arc stays **solid**, so the pair can't collapse into a single flat colour,
- a third pins the caller's palette choice — the half of the fix that doesn't live in `MacroRing`.

**Three mutations, each fails its test**: the groove restored, the track drawn at full strength, the caller back on the accents.

## Also: a flaky test made robust

`formArtOwnerRelease` SHA-256s every delivered frame of ten guides straight off disk — 109 ms alone, but real I/O that has now **twice** overrun vitest's 5 s default under full-suite load (8.7 s measured). Given an explicit 30 s budget. A default is a value nobody chose for a case doing that much work; this is not a re-run in disguise.

## Verification

Full unit suite green — **8508 passed**. `tsc -b` clean, lint 0 errors. Capture run going up alongside; the macro-tile frames should change and I'll check them rather than assume.

author: heshipstech
body:
## What this is

The owner's first RLDD re-derivation runs refused on missing blink logs — on *different* files per folder, which was the clue. Reading the corpus runner settled it: it clicks the blinks export **only when the button is enabled**, and a session with no blinks disables it, so **a zero-blink video writes no log by design**. The tool's refuse-on-any-absence rule conflated that with data loss.

## The discrimination

The seconds file itself is the witness, checked over the whole file because the blink log is session-wide:

- A filled `lastBlinkDurationMs` anywhere (sticky from the first blink on) or a `blinkRatePerMin` above zero anywhere proves a log was written → its absence is **loss**, refused by name with the evidence stated in the message.
- No evidence anywhere → the absent log **is** the zero-blink export: `blink_count = 0`, a measured rate of 0 over observed time, flagged in the output as `[no log: zero-blink export]` rather than silently blended with logged rows.

`RederivedRate` gains a `blink_log` field ("present" | "absent-no-blinks") so the source of every numerator travels with its number.

## Tests

Four added, watched failing first — two of them already passed under today's behavior (any absence refused), which is itself recorded in the commit: the discrimination narrows the refusal, it doesn't widen acceptance. The zero-blink case, the sticky-duration witness, the rate witness, and the source flag are each pinned. Python suite 521 collected (519 passed, 2 skipped), counts cascaded through analysis/collected-tests.txt, README and the status block.

## Gates

No src/ change. Python 519 passed 2 skipped; ruff check + format clean; JS suite 1656/1656 with coverage; counts:check ok; prettier clean.

author: anukuljha
body:
## What changes

Four things found while using the desktop app.

**A commented-out sandbox path the agent tried to `cd` into.** The
working-directory prompt took the cwd from the run and then wrote
`/workspace` into five more sentences beside it; the Agent Host's own native
fragment did it too, in the sentence warning against exactly that. A user
watched Claude Code run `cd /workspace/c/2026-09-10/…` in a native shell on a
Mac, where nothing is mounted at that root. The root is derived from the run's
cwd now, so there is one source for it.

**A sandbox download nobody asked for.** Starting called
`warm_sandbox_images` right after `ready`, so every start fetched several
hundred megabytes and raised a toast about it. Those images are for pod
workloads; someone whose coding agents run natively has nothing to put in a
sandbox and paid for it anyway. Starting reports instead of fetching, with a
new terminal `not-prepared` state so the workspace stops polling and the toast
stays quiet.

**Nowhere to set the sandbox up.** Runtime settings had no mention of it, so
a person who *did* want pod execution had no way to ask. It now has a panel
that says whether the image is here and offers the download only in the state
where the offer means anything.

**Copy did nothing, silently.** `navigator.clipboard` does not exist outside a
secure context, and the desktop workspace is served from an `http://*.localhost`
origin WKWebView does not trust — so reading `.writeText` threw a TypeError
before anything reached a clipboard. The message copy button caught that into
an empty block. Fixed at all 21 call sites, since the bug is the context.

## Why

All four were reported from real use of a nightly build.

## How to verify

```bash
make desktop-check
cd lemma-backend && uv run pytest app/modules/agent/tests/unit -q
cd lemma-frontend && npx vitest run lib/ && npx tsc --noEmit
```

Desktop check green; backend `1582 passed`; frontend `lib/` green with tsc clean.

Guards checked by breaking them rather than assumed:

| guard | with the fix disabled |
|---|---|
| the native fragment names no container root | fails |
| announcing never overwrites a fetch in flight | fails |
| copy works with no `navigator.clipboard` | fails (TypeError) |

## Notes

- Pods now fetch the sandbox image on first use rather than at startup, so the
  first pod task on a fresh install is slower. `sandbox.ensure` already handled
  that path; it is simply no longer pre-warmed unless asked.
- Removes a doc comment that appeared twice, verbatim, on one function.
- Pre-existing and not from this change:
  `components/auth/portal/auth/redirects.test.ts` times out under full-suite
  load (a dynamic `import()` against a 5s limit). It passes alone, and it still
  fails with this branch's new test file excluded.

## Checklist

- [x] Tests cover the behavioral change
- [x] Lint, typecheck, and architecture gates pass locally

---

## Also here: a message typed at an ACP turn is queued, and says so

Type at a running in-process agent and it gets the message — a capability
claims anything said mid-run and hands it to the model on its next step. Type
at an Agent Host agent and it does not. **ACP has no steering primitive**:
`session/prompt` is one request that returns when the turn ends, and 2.1.0
(released 2026-09-04) still has no method to add input to one in flight.

It was never lost — it was persisted at once and answered by a follow-up run
after the turn. That is a reasonable fallback and a bad thing to look at: the
transcript showed the message as sent while the agent could not see it, so it
read as ignored.

It is held now and named as held: a queued row with the sentence that explains
it, and two ways out — wait for the turn (the default, costs nothing) or
**Send now**, which stops the turn and delivers it. Interrupting discards the
agent's in-flight work, so it is a button rather than what typing does.

Notes on the shape:

- Which harness answers is a property of the **model**, not the conversation,
  so the branch reads `harness_kind` off the model catalogue.
- Only while a turn is really running. A test caught the first version
  queueing a message that had nothing to wait for.
- Send now stops and lets the transition drain the queue, because
  `STOP_REQUESTED` still counts as running — the queue waits for the stop to
  land rather than racing the turn it cancelled.
- The queue is sent client-side because a deliberate stop is exactly the case
  the backend's follow-up excludes, correctly: pressing stop is not a request
  for another turn. This needs **no API change** — `append_message` already
  starts a run when none is active.
- Queued messages live in `localStorage`, so leaving the page does not discard
  a promise the UI made. Guarding the accessor, not just the call: a browser
  set to block site data throws on `window.localStorage` itself.
- Attachments stay on the old path — their uploads would outlive a
  client-side hold.

```bash
cd lemma-typescript && npx vitest run src/__tests__/ && npx tsc --noEmit
cd lemma-frontend && npx vitest run && npx tsc --noEmit
```

SDK `313 passed` (41 files); frontend `1368 passed` (129 files); both tsc clean.

body:
Found by reading `RELEASE_PROCESS.md` and `RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md` end to end
against each other, at the maintainer's prompting. **Nothing watches for this
class:** `check:refs` verifies repo paths and npm script names, not §-references
between documents, nor whether a step's input exists at the moment the step asks
for it.

| # | Claim | Reality |
| - | ----- | ------- |
| 1 | §3: publishing the draft creates the tag "407 commits past" the built code | written 2026-09-08; `main` has gained 25 commits, so 432 today |
| 2 | checklist header: the process refers back "in its steps §1, §6 and §8" | §1, §2, §5, §6 and §8 — §5 was already missing |
| 3 | §2 step 4: the draft body is written before §9 exists | not established, and it contradicts §5 |
| 4 | §6: "match §9 as signed … (§2 step 4)" | mixes a checklist section and a section of this document |

## On each

1. **Deleted rather than updated.** The argument — that the tag would name a tree
   which never shipped — does not need a count, and a count nothing recomputes
   is wrong again tomorrow.
2. **Replaced by the property, not by a fresh enumeration.** "Wherever one of its
   steps needs per-candidate evidence" cannot go stale the way a list of numbers
   does; the list was already wrong when it was written.
3. §5 sits after the build, so if the smoke runs before the notes are written it
   can use the real §9. Reworded to say only what holds: whichever of the two is
   written before the smoke carries the provisional version.
4. A live hazard rather than a typo — **both documents number their sections
   1–8**, and the same bare number means different things in each (§6 is
   Approval in one and Sidecar lifecycle in the other).

## Not in this PR

Two structural findings from the same reading, because they change the shape of
both files rather than correcting a sentence:

- the checklist carries 12 per-candidate ticks in §1/§2 that nothing ever resets,
  while §3–§9 are recorded per candidate in the appendix;
- the manual smoke — the longest step in the whole release — has no step number
  in the document that owns the steps, appearing only as a precondition inside
  §6.

author: jcschaff
body:
## Decision this implements

Eran's semantics call (sms-ecoli#166, 2026-09-10 12:20Z): **adopt division semantics everywhere.** A generation ends at division on both dispatch paths, the founder of the next generation is the daughter *at division*, and no compute is spent on the abandoned sibling. This makes the single-window (Nextflow `LineageStep`) path match the tick-driven chain path and how vEcoli runs multigeneration lineages.

## What was wrong

On the single-window path `_run_until_division` ran the inner composite for the whole `max_duration_per_gen` window in one call. The mother divided (e.g. at 2,528 s), the Division step added both daughters, and the composite kept running them to the window end; the runner then carried daughter `00` aged (window − division) s past division. Sim 955's debug line proved it: `DIVISION at t=2528s` … `[lineage-debug] t=1072.0` (= 3,600 − 2,528), and the instrumented sim 956 stream showed it without any flag: `structure.changed` at 2,528, `run.end` at 3,600, `lineage.generation.end.duration` 1,072. The chain path, driven in 1 s ticks, observed the division on its tick and ended the generation there — two lineage semantics for one runner.

## Change

- `_run_until_division` runs the window in `division_poll_interval` slices (new config key, **default 10.0 s**) and breaks on the structural change (agents map changed) or the survivor's divide flag — the same two signals the post-run code already checked. Division-exception handling is unchanged. The tick-driven path (`interval=1`) still issues exactly one 1 s run.
- With the loop, the inner clock at break time is the division time to within one slice; `_elapsed_after_run` (#771's rule, carried here as a commit until #771 merges) makes that clock win over a daughter's stamp. **Residual: ≤ one slice** (10 s by default; `time_step`-sized slices remove it at the cost of one `run` call per tick).
- `division_poll_interval` is settable from a dispatch: forwarded by `LineageStep._FORWARDED`, declared in `LineageStep.config_schema` and `LineageProcess.config_schema`, exposed as a `workflow_nf` generator parameter / builder kwarg (applied only when set), with a reachability test beside the #730/#731/#732 structural tests.

## What changes for existing Nextflow campaigns

Every multigeneration Nextflow run becomes stop-at-division: `lineage_time_offset` = the sum of division times (as on chain), the founder is the daughter at division, generation wall time drops by the abandoned tail (≈30 % on 946's shape), and `summary.json` durations equal the division times. Runs completed under the old window semantics (898, 946, 951) booked full windows; their published history is unchanged but their cumulative-time arithmetic differs from post-#773 runs — say which semantics a comparison uses.

## Tests

`_DividingComposite` (divides at a scripted time and ages the daughters' own clocks): stops within one slice of a 2,528 s division in a 3,600 s window, books 2,528–2,538 s, carries the daughter at division, never runs more than one slice past it; tick-driven path unchanged (`calls == [1.0]`); no division consumes the full window and books it; the knob reaches every lineage node from a dispatch and stays absent when unset. Lineage/division/workflow_nf set: 128 passed on the named files, 274 passed in the `-k` subset (the one failure was the new reachability test's own document lookup, fixed in the last commit).

## Verification plan

One 1×5 of 898's shape on both paths on a pin carrying #769 + #771 + #773 (`bisect/769-771-773`), then the same dose-onset readout used for 951/952: expected first nonzero drug at cumulative ≈10,000 s on **both** paths, `duration == emits` per generation, and the `lineage.warning{check: duration_vs_emits}` from v2ecoli#772 silent.

body:
<!--
# nf-core/metatdenovo pull request

Many thanks for contributing to nf-core/metatdenovo!

Please fill in the appropriate checklist below (delete whatever is not relevant).
These are the most common things requested on pull requests (PRs).

Remember that PRs should be made against the dev branch, unless you're preparing a pipeline release.

Learn more about contributing: [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/nf-core/metatdenovo/tree/master/docs/CONTRIBUTING.md)
-->

## PR checklist

- [x] This comment contains a description of changes (with reason).
- [ ] If you've fixed a bug or added code that should be tested, add tests!
- [ ] If you've added a new tool - have you followed the pipeline conventions in the [contribution docs](https://github.com/nf-core/metatdenovo/tree/master/docs/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [ ] If necessary, also make a PR on the nf-core/metatdenovo _branch_ on the [nf-core/test-datasets](https://github.com/nf-core/test-datasets) repository.
- [x] Make sure your code lints (`nf-core pipelines lint`).
- [ ] Ensure the test suite passes (`nextflow run . -profile test,docker --outdir <OUTDIR>`).
- [ ] Check for unexpected warnings in debug mode (`nextflow run . -profile debug,test,docker --outdir <OUTDIR>`).
- [x] Usage Documentation in `docs/usage.md` is updated.
- [ ] Output Documentation in `docs/output.md` is updated.
- [x] `CHANGELOG.md` is updated.
- [ ] `README.md` is updated (including new tool citations and authors/contributors).

## Description

Docs-only PR, prompted by a real incident: a colleague's Megahit assembly ran for 6 days,
reached k=69, and was killed before finishing.

`-resume` doesn't help recover a task killed partway through: Nextflow's resume works at
the whole-task level (cached if it previously finished with exit code 0, otherwise not),
with no visibility into how far a killed task's own process actually got. A killed
`MEGAHIT` task simply isn't cached, so a plain `-resume` reruns it from scratch.

Megahit itself does have a real, independent checkpoint mechanism though --
`megahit --continue -o <out_dir>` reads `<out_dir>/checkpoints.txt`/`options.json` and
resumes from the last fully-completed step, skipping everything before it. Verified this
directly rather than trusting the `--help` blurb: read Megahit's own Python source to
confirm exactly what `--continue` does and doesn't restore (it re-reads `-t`/`-m` from the
original invocation too, ignoring anything passed alongside `--continue` -- so the recovery
environment needs at least as much CPU/RAM as the original task had), then reproduced it
end to end -- ran a synthetic assembly, killed it mid-k-mer-stage, and confirmed
`--continue` logged `passing check point N` for every already-completed step and picked up
exactly where it left off, rather than restarting.

New section in `docs/large_datasets.md`, "Recovering a Megahit run that was killed partway
through": a practical, work-directory-first recipe -- find the failed task's work dir,
confirm there's a checkpoint, resume Megahit itself (Docker/Singularity/native examples),
then hand the finished assembly back to the pipeline via the existing `--user_assembly`
param rather than trying to trick Nextflow's own cache into treating the task as complete.
Linked from `docs/usage.md`'s "Assembler options" and `-resume` sections.

_Reviewed and drafted with some help from Claude Code._

body:
## spec 34 §8.2 — the tebako product repo's Windows signing leg

The release workflow's `windows` (ucrt64) job gains the spec 34 signing
chain, armed by the repo variable `WINDOWS_SIGNING_ENABLED=true` and
byte-identical to today when disarmed (spec 00 invariant 7).

**Chain (in order, between stage and the ship gate):**

1. **Arm check** (`ci/windows-sign-gate.sh`, §4/§7.5) — disarmed: loud
   notice + skip everything; armed with any of the six §3 values empty:
   named `::error::` listing exactly which, before any signing call.
2. **Azure login** (§5) — `azure/login@v2`, OIDC workload identity; the
   job carries `id-token: write` + `environment: windows-signing`, the
   §3/§5 attestation boundary (unsigned runs never request a token).
3. **Sign** — `Azure/artifact-signing-action@v1`, in place over
   `tebako-rs/out`, filter `exe,dll` (§7.3: enumerate by extension,
   never a name list), SHA256 digests, RFC 3161 timestamp
   (`http://timestamp.acs.microsoft.com`, §1.4).
4. **Verify** (§7.1/§7.2) — pwsh: `signtool verify /pa /v` exit 0 +
   timestamp evidence in verbose output, cross-checked with
   `Get-AuthenticodeSignature` (`Status=Valid`, `TimeStamperCertificate`
   non-null) per staged exe; any miss fails the leg naming the artifact.
5. **Re-hash** (`ci/windows-sign-refrag.sh`, §1.3 sign-then-hash) —
   recomputes the `frag-windows-ucrt64` sha256/size fragments over the
   SIGNED bytes so finalize's SHA256SUMS / sidecars / manifest anchor
   what ships. Fails loudly on a staged exe with no fragment (stage.sh
   drift), a non-conforming name, or an empty `out/`.

The ship gate then smokes the signed exes with PATH scrubbed — the
on-platform proof that the signed artifacts run.

**Deviations from the spec's draft shape** (documented in the workflow
comments): `Azure/artifact-signing-action@v1`, not the draft's `@v0` —
the mandated `signing-account-name` input exists only at v1 (`@v0`
carries only the deprecated `trusted-signing-account-name`); signtool
is resolved from the action's real BuildTools cache
(`%LOCALAPPDATA%\TrustedSigning\…`, module still named TrustedSigning at
v1) with the ArtifactSigning spelling as forward-compat, then Windows
Kits, newest first. Both new actions carry `# TODO(sha-pin): pin on
first armed run` — deliberate: the sha is recorded from the first armed
run's evidence.

**Validation:** `bash -n` both scripts; YAML parse + `actionlint` clean;

PR3 del programa Círculos: la participación real, **corregida tras tres rondas
de auditoría** y detenida en Draft para la auditoría final.

```

BASE=main

RAILWAY_STAGED_CHANGES_TOUCHED=false
BLOCKS_READY_OR_MERGE_PENDING_RECONCILIATION=true
ACCOUNT_DELETION_WITH_CIRCLE_EVENTS=blocked_pending_sanctioned_scrub_design
REQUIRED_BEFORE_PILOT=true
```

---

## Ronda 3 — los cuatro hallazgos

**`on` omitía la membresía del invitante.** `assertInviterEligible` y
`lockAndAssertInviter` retornaban temprano bajo `on` — «no hay allowlist que
consultar» se leyó como «no hay nada que comprobar» — mientras la ruta de
participación de PR3 revalida al invitante en todos los modos. El sistema se
contradecía donde una persona lo nota: un miembro crea la invitación y se va,
el enlace sigue inspeccionando como usable, el canje consume la invitación,
acepta el asiento, mueve la actividad a `PREPARING`, crea la sesión y escribe
eventos, y el primer comando del invitado lo rechaza. Alguien acepta, ve en la
pantalla del otro que el Dúo empezó, y no puede hacer nada — con todo ya
escrito. Hoy la membresía es independiente del modo; sólo la allowlist es
exclusiva de `pilot`, y ambas rutas comparten un único predicado.

**Una confirmación exitosa no comprometía su clave.** Confirmar el artefacto A
con K1 y repetirlo con K2 devolvía éxito saltándose el append, así que K2 nunca
quedaba registrada: el llamante podía creer que K2 significaba «confirmé A», y
K2 seguía libre para gastarse después en B. Una clave, dos significados
exitosos, ningún registro del primero. Hoy se rechaza con
`CIRCLE_IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`: una clave se gasta sólo cuando un recibo la
registra.

**La idempotencia caducaba con el catálogo.** `createDuo` resolvía la plantilla
antes de consultar el recibo, así que una petición que ya había creado un Dúo
dejaba de ser reproducible en cuanto editorial archivaba esa versión — un
reintento de timeout recibía `CIRCLE_TEMPLATE_UNAVAILABLE` por un recurso que
existe. Un replay no instancia nada y no necesita la plantilla: la actividad
comprometida lleva el pin que decide replay de conflicto.

**El test de expiración no demostraba su precondición.** Fijaba
`expiresAt = createdAt + 1s` y afirmaba que el comando funciona — lo que también
pasa en una construcción que sí re-verifica la expiración. Hoy la fecha se mueve
inequívocamente al pasado y el test afirma desde PostgreSQL, antes del comando,
que la invitación está vencida y la sesión vigente y no revocada; un control
complementario expira la sesión para demostrar cuál gobierna.

Y el comentario de `CircleShareConfirmation`: la unión tiene **tres** miembros.
`WITHDRAW` es un comando separado.

---

## El `green=false` del control 9

El arnés no conservó ese log, así que corrí el mismo gate sobre el baseline
limpio y lo reproduje: **tres corridas consecutivas con carga 11.7, una falló.**

```
CONTROL_9_RESTORE_FAILURE_CAUSE=foreign_preexisting_intermittent_test
```

El test intermitente es `src/guide/guide-firewall.e2e-spec.ts` — **ajeno a
Círculos** — que devuelve 404 en `POST /api/guide/sessions` al resolver el
catálogo de Guide. PR3 no toca ni un archivo de Guide. No es fichero sin
restaurar, ni `dist` obsoleto, ni proceso o transacción abandonada, ni colisión
de bases efímeras, ni test de Círculos, ni timeout: es una suite ajena que
falla de vez en cuando, y la corrida de restauración la arrastraba porque
ejecutaba **todos** los pg-spec del repositorio.

Ese flake podía corromper un control en las dos direcciones: marcar
`green=false` con el baseline sano, o marcar `RED_WRONG_REASON` por un fallo
de otro. Siguiendo la instrucción de no tocar suites ajenas dentro de PR3, el
bucle de controles pasó a usar la **suite focalizada de Círculos** (143 tests,
9 s en vez de 95 s). La suite PostgreSQL completa sigue corriendo, una vez, en
los gates finales: acotar el bucle de control no es acotar la evidencia.

Limpieza de la corrida interrumpida: una base efímera huérfana
(`pg_locks_30741`), **cero** conexiones, **cero** transacciones abiertas, cero
procesos vivos, árbol byte-idéntico al baseline. La corrida interrumpida queda
descartada, no contada.

---

## Controles negativos

```
ORIGINAL_PR3_NEGATIVE_CONTROLS=20/20_historical
CORRECTIVE_NEGATIVE_CONTROLS=21/21_final_baseline
ALL_41_MUTATIONS_RERUN_ON_FINAL_BASELINE=false
FINAL_NEGATIVE_CONTROL_BASELINE=4167cb1455838912cd8ea5d28cccb4eb56665b1e
FINAL_TREE_MATCHES_BASELINE=true
INTERRUPTED_RUN_COUNTED=false
```

Los 20 originales se verificaron contra un HEAD anterior y **no** se han vuelto
a mutar contra este baseline. La suite verde demuestra que aquellos ratchets
siguen activos; eso no es lo mismo que repetir sus mutaciones, y sumarlos como
41 sería inventar cobertura.

Los controles 17 y 21 están separados a propósito: mutan rutas distintas
(`assertInviterEligible` y `lockAndAssertInviter`) y fallan por tests distintos.
`exchange` consulta la ruta rápida antes que la autoritativa, así que mutar sólo
una de ellas no cambia el resultado de la otra salvo en la carrera — juntarlas
bajo un mismo test habría sido cómodo y falso.

---

## Compuertas

| Compuerta | Resultado |
|---|---|
| Círculos focalizado (unit) | 205 pasan · 13 archivos |
| API unitaria | 3133 pasan · **0 fallan** · 221 archivos |

author: kpenfound
body:
Closes #50.

Retrieval over L1: an embedding column on the document table, a full-text index
on `raw_text`, and `l1.Store.Search` — the two halves ranked over what the
caller may read and fused by reciprocal rank. It returns documents, not
answers, and it is a callable function with no interface in front of it, which
is what #52 needs.

## What is here

**Three migrations**, because a column and two indexes are three purposes:
`vector(1536)` on `l1_docs` (7), a GIN index over `to_tsvector('english',
raw_text)` (8), and a `jsonb_path_ops` index on `acl` (9), which every read
filters on before it ranks anything.

**The write path.** `Store.Put` clears a document's embedding whenever it
writes different `text`, so a vector cannot outlive the words it was made from
and "what needs embedding" is "what has no vector". `Store.Embed` fills that in
through the `embed` tier and compare-and-sets on the text it embedded, which
needs no ordering between two writers. The distiller calls it after every write
— so a re-distillation that changed nothing makes no embedding call — and
refuses at startup a tier whose vectors are not the width of the column
(`llm.CheckDimensions`, which nothing called until now).

**The read path.** `Store.Search(ctx, reader, opts)`: similarity over the
embedding of `text`, Postgres full text over `raw_text`, fused by RRF with
k=60. The filter is *inside both halves* rather than around the result — a
document the caller may not read never takes a rank, so it can neither be
returned nor push a readable one out of the candidate window. `l1.ReaderFor` is
the one place a caller's grants are derived from the identity mapping
(`principal.Resolver.Teams` and `Claims` are new).

No new dependencies; still the three ADR-named ones.

## Round 2: what the review found

**1. The fail-open (finding 1) is fixed in code, not documented away.** A
reader's audience took a principal's handle *and* its folded form as
access-list entries alongside their native id, and the mapping keeps those two
namespaces apart on purpose — so a handle that folds to somebody else's native
id is not a claim conflict and `NewResolver` accepts it. The reviewer's repro
(alice `{u1, alice}`, mallory `{u2, U1}`) made a document shared with alice
readable by mallory.

The rule now: **a configured native id is a grant as it stands** — an entry's
`native_id` is the source's id for the thing, and two principals cannot claim
one native id — and **a handle is a grant only where nobody else answers to
that spelling in either namespace**. The question is answered by
`principal.Resolver.Claims`, which asks the mapping's own ambiguity machinery
(`lookup`, the same one `Resolve` uses) rather than comparing bare strings, so
there is one place that knows how the two namespaces overlap. It still fails
closed in the direction that matters: a genuinely ambiguous mapping costs a
person a document they may read, and never grants one they may not.
`internal/l1/reader.go`'s comment says this, and the README carries the rule.
`TestReaderForRefusesASpellingTwoPrincipalsAnswerTo` is the reviewer's repro,
extended to the group case (a team whose name is somebody's native id), with
alice keeping every grant of her own as the positive control.

**2, 4, 5 — the prose.** `Search`'s doc no longer claims an empty audience
reads nothing (public is public; it is the missing *principal* that reads
nothing), and `Reader`'s zero-value sentence gives that reason instead. The
label rule the three sites cite `(internal/l1)` for is now in that README,
beside the namespace rule above. `Reader` says why this filter reads
`Grant.Scopes` and not `Grant.Rights.Read`: the read *reach* is #21's, and a
filter guessing at it now would be a permission nobody granted or a denial
nobody asked for.

**3 — ADR-0005 and design.md.** ADR-0005's "reads have no model in the loop" is
carried in the status column of `docs/adr/README.md`, the way #42's, #62's and
#63's deviations are; the three tiers themselves are unchanged, and `embed` on
the read path is the same tier doing the same job. Grepping the *claim* rather
than the sentence turned up a fourth site the review did not name —
`internal/service/api`'s package comment said "there is no model in the read
path" — which is now correct.

> **For a person: `docs/design.md:30` says "Reads are structured lookups with no
> model in the loop", and this issue makes that false.** Embedding the query is
> what `search(scope, query)` is; the design doc's own API table asks for it. I
> have left the line alone because design.md is normative product text rather
> than mine to edit — it needs one sentence saying the read path embeds a query
> and generates nothing.

## Choices I made

All eleven were ruled on in round 1 and stand: 1 `vector(1536)`; 2 no chunking,
`MaxEmbedBytes`; 3 no ANN index; 4 `raw_text` only, `english` named everywhere;
5 `websearch_to_tsquery` and its AND semantics; 6 the audience is the human's;
7 a grant is (kind, source, native id), label ignored — **now narrowed by round
2's fix: the spellings a caller holds are its native ids plus every handle
nobody else answers to**; 8 scope optional, an ungranted scope returns nothing;
9 `DefaultSearchLimit` 20, `SearchCandidates` 200, `MaxSearchLimit` 200; 10 an
embedding failure fails the distill job; 11 no CLI subcommand.

## How I tested it

`dagger check` — all 8 green, exit 0, unit total 793 → 863. `go vet` under both
build configurations, `-race` with `-tags=integration` against Postgres,
`go mod tidy` clean. `hearsay:integration-test` came back faster than last
round, so I proved it still runs by breaking one assertion in
`TestSearchNeverReturnsADocumentTheReaderMayNotRead` and watching the check
fail.

The two acceptance criteria are integration tests in
`internal/l1/search_integration_test.go`:

- `TestSearchFusesWhatEachHalfFinds`: a document with the query's words and no
  embedding comes back with a text rank and no vector rank; a document with no
  word of the query and an embedding the query embeds to comes back with a
  vector rank and no text rank; a document both halves find outscores either;
  a document holding only some of the query's words does not appear.
- `TestSearchNeverReturnsADocumentTheReaderMayNotRead`: the private document is
  the best match both halves have, and it appears at no rank at all — the
  readable one is rank 1 in *both* halves, which is what "filtered before
  ranking" means. The positive control is the same query by somebody in that
  group, holding the grant under a different label.

### Mutation testing

Round 1's 35 mutations were re-run against the changed code: **35/35 still
killed.** Ten more over round 2's logic, 9 killed:

| Mutation | Verdict |
|---|---|
| A handle is a grant whoever else answers to it | killed |
| A spelling nobody answers to is a grant | killed |
| The raw / the folded spelling of a handle is not offered | killed (×2) |
| A configured native id is not a grant | killed |
| A team's grants are derived under the reader's own id | killed |
| `Claims` reads only the native-id namespace / only the handle namespace | killed (×2) |
| `Claims` answers for an ambiguous spelling | killed |
| Somebody else's spelling is a grant (`!ok \|\| claimed != owner` → `&&`) | **survived** |

Two survivors on the first pass; one of them — a guard in `Claims` for an empty
source or spelling — was the branch being redundant rather than untested, since
the mapping indexes neither, so it is deleted in its own commit.

The one left is an equivalent mutant for reachable inputs. `entriesFor` is
always called with the identity's own principal as `owner`, so a spelling either
names that principal (`ok`, `claimed == owner`) or is ambiguous (`!ok`,
`claimed == ""`); "unambiguously somebody else" cannot arise, which makes
`!ok && claimed != owner` the same predicate as `!ok`. The `claimed != owner`
half is not dead code — it is what makes the `owner` argument load-bearing, and
the mutation tha

author: jasiek
body:
## What changed

The channel toolbar's **Actions** dropdown is gone. Every action it held is now its own button, in one wrapping row:

```
[+] [−] [↑] [↓] │ [✂] [⧉] [📋] │ 🇺🇸 GMRS  🇺🇸 FRS  🇪🇺 PMR446 │ Repeaters  🇪🇺 przemienniki.net  🌍 repeaterbook.com  🇮🇪 IRTS  🇬🇧 RSGB
```

- **Clipboard actions** (cut / copy / paste) are icon-only.
- **Band plans** (GMRS, FRS, PMR446) and the four **repeater directories** carry the flag of the country or region they cover, since a flag alone does not say what an import contains.
- Every button has a `title` spelling that out — e.g. *"United Kingdom: query the RSGB ETCC repeater directory"*, *"Europe: add the 16 licence-free PMR446 simplex channels, 446 MHz"*.
- The four repeater buttons sit in a `role="group"` labelled **Repeaters**, so the heading reaches assistive technology as the group name rather than being a caption only sighted users get.

All seven icon buttons are inline SVG rather than emoji. Emoji has no glyph that reads as *copy* — 📋 and 📥 both stand for containers, not actions — so the clipboard trio uses the conventional line art, and the four editing buttons moved with them rather than leave the toolbar mixing coloured emoji with monochrome strokes.

## Why

Two clicks and a scan of a nine-item popup to reach an action that fits on the toolbar. The dropdown also hid *which* directories exist, which is most of what a new user needs to know.

Stroking the icons with `currentColor` fixes a second thing: an icon now follows its button's text colour, so it greys out when the button is disabled and stays legible in the dark theme. Emoji did neither — a disabled ➖ stayed full-colour while its label greyed out, reading as a live button.

## Notes for review

- **Deleted machinery:** the menu toggle, popup, outside-click close, and the Escape branch that shut it, plus `setMenuOpen` — which was on `channel-table.js`'s public surface and called by two siblings through `ctx.table` (`repeater-query.js` closed the menu behind its modal; `ui.js` gave Escape a fallback).
- **Import wiring is untouched.** `repeater-query.js` binds through `dom[source.toolbarButton]`, a config string, so keeping the `#channel-import-*` ids carried the whole thing across the rewrite. The field was renamed `menuButton` → `toolbarButton`, which is now accurate.
- **`aria-describedby` was deliberately avoided** on the repeater buttons: pointing them at the group label would have suppressed each `title` as the accessible description, losing exactly the detail the tooltips exist to carry. The `role="group"` wrapper gives the heading to screen readers *and* leaves the titles intact.
- **Band-plan tooltips name channel counts** (30 GMRS, 22 FRS, 16 PMR446) read off `web/js/datasources.js`. Nothing pins them, so editing those tables would leave the tooltips stale.
- **On a phone the toolbar becomes four rows** (~198px tall, no horizontal overflow at 375px). That's the honest cost of a flat toolbar over a dropdown.
- **Screenshots not regenerated.** `images/screenshot.png` and the social-preview images still show the old menu; per `CLAUDE.md` those are refreshed on `master`, not on a branch.

## New dependencies

None.

## Testing

- Full suite green: `npm test` — 550 / 161 / 562 / 23, zero failures.
- `tests/channels/ui-repeater-modal.mjs` lost its assertion that the RSGB modal closed the actions menu, and `tests/support/fake-dom.mjs` lost the two stubs for the removed elements.
- Verified in the browser: GMRS inserts its 30 rows, Insert adds rows through the new SVG-bearing button, the RSGB modal opens from its button and still closes on Escape, and the icons render correctly at 4× in both light and dark themes with disabled buttons dimming as intended.

body:
## Le relevé

Titre → **« Les principales menaces cyber IA »**. Le chapeau explique la chaîne : une requête traverse cinq maillons — l'invite, les données, le modèle, les actions, l'humain — et une menace existe à chaque maillon.

**La chaîne cesse d'être une légende et devient le filtre.** Un maillon cliqué ne montre que les menaces qui entrent par lui. Le geste et l'explication sont la même chose : le lecteur apprend la structure de la surface d'attaque en s'en servant.

Deux choix qui comptent :

- chaque maillon porte **son compte avant le clic** — filtrer ne doit pas être une surprise ;
- chaque maillon est un `<button>`, pas un `<li>` cliquable : le rôle, le focus clavier et l'annonce de l'état pressé viennent du navigateur au lieu d'attributs qu'il faudrait penser à écrire.

Un test de navigateur tient le mécanisme : il lit le compte annoncé, clique, vérifie que le nombre de rangées tombe **exactement** à ce compte, puis que le filtre se relâche. Sans ce dernier contrôle, un filtre sans sortie passerait au vert.

## Trois coupes

| | |
| --- | --- |
| la capture de `make demo` dans la section | retirée |
| « Deux offres. La différence est technique avant d'être commerciale. » | **« Deux offres »** — les deux lignes de qualification disent déjà à qui |
| « Et, tout aussi clairement, pour qui ce n'est pas » | retirée |

Les gardes partent avec ce qu'ils gardaient, **et seulement eux** : le contrôle qui exigeait la capture sur la page, et le test de navigateur du plafond.

Les gardes de l'**enregistrement** restent entiers : `AD-26` tient toujours, `scripts/record_demo.py` refuse d'écrire quand la démonstration échoue, et `tests/test_demo_capture.py` le vérifie encore.

author: malwareuniverse-hue
body:
## Summary

Five Remotion compositions, each mapped frame-by-frame to a transcript segment and registered in `Root.tsx`. Every scene is self-contained (`timeline.ts`, `theme.ts`, `utils.ts`, `fonts.ts` plus its components) and follows the locked PBM visual system.

## Scenes

| Composition | Length | Place at | Ground |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GuestMindset` | 500f | `00:00:01:14` | PBM near-black |
| `SubscribeCTA` | 390f | `00:00:16:19` | transparent (alpha) |
| `ChapterThree` | 210f | `00:00:29:11` | PBM near-black |
| `FiveThings` | 1200f | `00:00:00:01` | chroma green (prop) |
| `AssessmentCTA` | 640f | `00:00:00:00` | chroma green (prop) |

- **GuestMindset** — the two things the guest is not weighing get struck through and recede, the question they actually ask takes the frame, then it resolves to the revenue-problem statement.
- **SubscribeCTA** — lower-left card on a transparent background so Emile stays on camera. The headline swaps once on the subscribe beat; the card grows per beat so it never shows space for words not yet spoken.
- **ChapterThree** — reusable chapter opener: ghost numeral, gold rule, gold label, two-line headline. Only the numeral, label and headline change between chapters.
- **FiveThings** — the five-check framework as a left-side panel, each check revealing on its cue with its question beneath. Header swaps to the framework lockup; a footer resolves the segment.
- **AssessmentCTA** — same panel geometry as `FiveThings`. Three outcomes, then the link block, then the closing contrast (muted gray for the habit, gold for the answer).

Each `timeline.ts` carries the source timecode and the local frame every transcript line lands on, so placement doesn't need re-deriving.

## Colour

All five scenes use only the six locked PBM roles — near-black `#0B0C0E`, charcoal `#1B1D21`, warm gold `#C9A45C`, soft white `#F3F1EC`, muted gray `#A7A7A5`, deep navy `#172033` — or one of them at a different opacity. Each `theme.ts` states that rule so it stays that way.

Note that the repo's seven earlier scenes are still on the previous teal/amber/rose palette, so the two sets will read as different systems if cut together. Moving them across is deliberately **not** in this PR.

## Chroma key

`FiveThings` and `AssessmentCTA` are built for a keyer rather than merely rendered on green: each panel is a fully opaque surface that wipes in by *height* and slides out, and every fade happens against charcoal inside it, so nothing is drawn over the green at partial opacity. Measured at 49–50 blended pixels out of 2,073,600, and the same count mid-wipe and mid-exit as when settled.

Since green is the lossiest of the options, the ground is a prop:

```
npx remotion render FiveThings out/FiveThings.mp4          # green, default
npx remotion render FiveThings out/FiveThings.mov \
  --props='{"backdrop":"transparent"}' \
  --codec=prores --prores-profile=4444 \
  --pixel-format=yuva444p10le --image-format=png           # true alpha
npx remotion render FiveThings out/FiveThings.mp4 \
  --props='{"backdrop":"dark"}'                            # full-screen cut
```

`SubscribeCTA` renders transparent; it needs the same `--pixel-format`/`--image-format` flags, or ProRes flattens the alpha away.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (eslint + tsc) passes, and all five compositions render end to end. The alpha variants were confirmed to carry a real alpha channel (`yuva444p12le`) rather than a flattened one.

The repo has no `.github/workflows`, so there is no CI on this PR — the above is the only verification it has.

## Wording to confirm before this ships

- `FiveThings`: the transcript's "pricing by **mirror** framework" is rendered on screen as **THE PRICING BY MIRA FRAMEWORK**.
- `AssessmentCTA`: `pricingbymira.com` is blocked by the authoring session's network egress policy, so the assessment's on-page name and button wording could not be read. Nothing on screen is copied from the site — the header uses the transcript's own words rather than a product name, and the only site-derived string is the URL itself. Flagged in `src/AssessmentCTA/timeline.ts`.
- On-screen copy is condensed to 4–10 words per the PBM system, so it is not verbatim transcript. All wording lives in the `timeline.ts` constants.

author: viv1kk
body:
Extends the pipeline from "CI proves the source" to "the running container is the code that passed".

## What this does

Push to `main` → CI proves the source → both images are built, **run**, and only then pushed to Docker Hub → Watchtower on the deployment machine notices the new digest and recreates `web`.

No ssh key, no inbound port. The poll is outbound, the same direction as the tunnel.

## Only `web` updates itself

| | Auto-updates | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `web` | yes | Recreating Nginx drops inbound connections and nothing else |
| `backend` | no | Recreating it destroys **every live room**, document and upload |
| `tunnel` | no | Its version is pinned deliberately |

The backend is still built, tested and published every push — it waits to be promoted at a chosen moment. Unattended room destruction at an unpredictable time is a very different thing from a restart someone chose.

## Safety

- **The artifact is proven, not just the source.** The image is built, **run**, and probed before any push. The backend check mounts the loop-backed ext4 filesystem and creates a room; the web check asserts `index.html` references `/assets/`, because an empty `dist/` still returns 200. A bad image fails here instead of becoming the tag a machine is polling.
- **Rollback is a re-tag, not a rebuild.** Every commit keeps an immutable `sha-` tag, so the *Roll back* workflow re-points `:latest` inside the registry — no rebuild, no ssh. Watchtower then applies it by the same path a deploy takes.
- **Two Docker Hub tokens.** Read/write for CI; read-only for the socket-mounted Watchtower container, which is root-equivalent on that host.

## Verified rather than assumed

Tested against a real Docker daemon:

- Label scoping: `scanned=1` of 5 containers, `scanned=2` once a second was labelled — the backend really is out of scope.
- Full update loop: new digest detected → graceful SIGQUIT stop → recreated → old image cleaned up → still serving 200.
- Ports and labels survive a Watchtower recreate, and the container stays watched afterwards, so updates repeat.
- Both smoke tests run against real builds: the ext4 loop mount comes up and `/api/storage` reports it.

Two findings worth recording:

- **`containrrr/watchtower` is unusable on Docker Engine 29.** Its last release defaults to Docker API v1.25; the daemon refuses anything below v1.40, and it fails with a nil-pointer panic rather than a clean error. This pins the maintained `nickfedor` fork, which negotiates the version itself (observed on v1.55) and reads the same label.
- **SHAs cannot simply be pinned everywhere.** Watchtower detects updates by re-resolving a *fixed tag name*; an immutable tag's digest never changes, so a pinned stack polls forever, looks healthy, and does nothing.

## Inert until switched on

`PUBLISH_IMAGES` is unset, so `images` is skipped and nothing publishes. `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` are already set.

**One-time cost when adopting:** the first `docker compose up -d` on this branch recreates the backend, because the image *name* changes — which drops every live room. Worth doing at a quiet moment.
